core: the greenhouse effect as well-established physics: shortwave solar radiation passes through the atmosphere; the surface re-radiates longwave (infrared) heat; greenhouse gases absorb most of it and re-radiate, slowing heat loss to space
the human-caused strengthening of the greenhouse effect: burning fossil fuels adds carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases, trapping more heat

observed changes with exact source framing: global average temperature rise (IPCC 1.09 [0.95 to 1.20] C in 2011-2020 vs 1850-1900; NASA 1.19 C / 2.14 F above 1951-1980 in 2025), ice loss (Arctic sea ice about 40 percent September decline; glacier retreat), sea level rise (IPCC 0.20 [0.15 to 0.25] m 1901-2018; NOAA 8-9 inches since 1880)

attribution: the IPCC's statement that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land, with its calibrated confidence language (virtually certain 99-100%, extremely likely 95-100%, very likely 90-100%, likely 66-100%)

projections depend on emissions scenarios: 2081-2100 warming very likely 1.0-1.8 C (SSP1-1.9), 2.1-3.5 C (SSP2-4.5), 3.3-5.7 C (SSP5-8.5); sea level likely 0.28-0.55 m (SSP1-1.9) to 0.63-1.01 m (SSP5-8.5) by 2100
impacts stated generally and factually: more frequent and intense hot extremes, increased heavy precipitation over most land since the 1950s, continuing sea level rise
mitigation and adaptation defined as the two broad categories of response, general education only, no policy advocacy
supporting: current atmospheric CO2: 410 ppm in 2019 (IPCC, highest in at least 2 million years); 429 ppm July 2026 (NASA citing NOAA Mauna Loa)
the Sun cannot explain the current warming (NASA)
human-caused warming quantified: likely range 0.8 to 1.3 C, best estimate 1.07 C (IPCC WGI)
temperature anomalies are always relative to a stated baseline (1951-1980 for NASA, 1850-1900 for IPCC)
the climate topic (sibling) owns what climate is and its classification; this lesson covers the current long-term change
outOfScope: climate definition and classification (sibling topic: climate)
weather and weather systems (sibling topic: weather)
atmosphere-ocean coupling, ENSO, and ocean circulation (sibling topics: atmosphere-and-oceans, ocean-circulation)
glacier physics and ice-sheet mechanics (sibling topic: glaciers; referenced only as an observed change)
climate policy, specific regulations, or individualized advice (general education only)
climate models, their construction, and internal technical detail

claims.claim: The greenhouse effect is well-established physics: about half the light energy reaching Earth's atmosphere passes through the air and clouds to the surface, where it is absorbed and radiated as infrared heat, and about 90 percent of that heat is then absorbed by greenhouse gases and re-radiated, slowing heat loss to space.

The greenhouse effect is essential to life on Earth, but human-made emissions are trapping and slowing heat loss to space; the key greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, methane, chlorofluorocarbons, and water vapor, and the evidence shows the current warming cannot be explained by the Sun.

It is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land; human activities, principally through emissions of greenhouse gases, have unequivocally caused global warming, with global surface temperature reaching 1.1 C above 1850-1900 in 2011-2020.

Global surface temperature was 1.09 [0.95 to 1.20] C higher in 2011-2020 than in 1850-1900, with larger increases over land than over the ocean, and each of the last four decades has been successively warmer than any decade that preceded it since 1850.
The likely range of total human-caused global surface temperature increase from 1850-1900 to 2010-2019 is 0.8 C to 1.3 C, with a best estimate of 1.07 C.

The 10 most recent years are the warmest on record: global temperatures in 2025 averaged 2.14 degrees Fahrenheit (1.19 degrees Celsius) above the 1951-1980 average, and the hottest year on record since modern recordkeeping began in 1880 remains 2024 (NASA/GISS).

Atmospheric CO2 measured 410 parts per million in 2019, higher than at any time in at least 2 million years (IPCC, high confidence); NASA's carbon dioxide vital-signs page reports a latest measurement of 429 ppm (July 2026).

Global mean sea level increased by 0.20 [0.15 to 0.25] m between 1901 and 2018; the average rate of sea level rise increased from 1.3 [0.6 to 2.1] mm per year in 1901-1971 to 1.9 [0.8 to 2.9] mm per year in 1971-2006 and 3.7 [3.2 to 4.2] mm per year in 2006-2018, and human influence was very likely the main driver of these increases since at least 1971.
Global average sea level has risen 8-9 inches (21-24 cm) since 1880, mostly from meltwater from glaciers and ice sheets plus thermal expansion of seawater (NOAA Climate.gov).

Human influence is very likely the main driver of the global retreat of glaciers since the 1990s and of the decrease in Arctic sea ice area between 1979-1988 and 2010-2019 (about 40 percent decrease in September and about 10 percent in March).

Global surface temperature will continue to increase until at least mid-century under all emissions scenarios considered; warming averaged over 2081-2100 relative to 1850-1900 is very likely to be 1.0 to 1.8 C under the very low emissions scenario (SSP1-1.9), 2.1 to 3.5 C under the intermediate scenario (SSP2-4.5), and 3.3 to 5.7 C under the very high emissions scenario (SSP5-8.5).
Likely global mean sea level rise by 2100 relative to 1995-2014 is 0.28-0.55 m under the SSP1-1.9 emissions scenario and 0.63-1.01 m under SSP5-8.5 (medium confidence).

It is virtually certain that hot extremes (including heatwaves) have become more frequent and more intense across most land regions since the 1950s, with high confidence that human-induced climate change is the main driver of these changes; the frequency and intensity of heavy precipitation events have increased since the 1950s over most land area for which observations are sufficient.

IPCC likelihood terms are calibrated: virtually certain means 99-100 percent probability, very likely 90-100 percent, likely 66-100 percent, and extremely likely 95-100 percent; square brackets [x to y] around a range mark the assessed very likely (90 percent) interval.

Responses to climate change fall into two broad categories: mitigation, which reduces greenhouse gas emissions or enhances their removal from the atmosphere, and adaptation, which adjusts to actual or expected climate change; the IPCC frames climate-resilient development as integrating adaptation and mitigation.

positions: IPCC reports warming relative to the 1850-1900 pre-industrial reference period (e.g., 1.09 [0.95 to 1.20] C for 2011-2020).
NASA GISS reports anomalies relative to its 1951-1980 baseline (1.19 C in 2025).
Popular writing sometimes mixes the two, producing inconsistent-looking numbers.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson always attaches the reference period to each number and explains that anomalies are meaningless without their baseline; the NASA figure is quoted with the 1951-1980 baseline and the IPCC figures with 1850-1900.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Sea level rise totals differ between sources.
positions: IPCC: global mean sea level increased 0.20 [0.15 to 0.25] m between 1901 and 2018 (about 8 inches).
NOAA Climate.gov: global average sea level risen 8-9 inches (21-24 cm) since 1880.
Different start dates (1880 vs 1901) and slightly different data sets explain the small spread.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both figures are stated with their own source and time period; no attempt is made to reconcile them into a single number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: CO2 concentration readings differ by date.
positions: IPCC: 410 ppm in 2019 (highest in at least 2 million years).
NASA vital signs: 429 ppm, latest measurement July 2026.
The rise of roughly 19 ppm in about seven years is consistent with the measured multi-year trend.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Each figure is quoted with its date and source; the lesson presents the rising trend rather than a single ambiguous number.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Some public claims dispute human attribution of recent warming.
positions: IPCC AR6: it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land (and the likely human-caused warming is 0.8-1.3 C, best estimate 1.07 C).
Claims that the Sun or natural variability explain recent warming, which NASA's causes page addresses by noting the evidence shows the current warming cannot be explained by the Sun.
The IPCC notes natural drivers changed global surface temperature by only -0.1 to +0.1 C over 1850-1900 to 2010-2019 (WGI A.1.3).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the IPCC's attribution statement and confidence language verbatim in framing, attributes the Sun-vs-warming point to NASA, and does not present natural-variability claims as equivalent.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained no substantive factual claims about climate change: its 'foundational concept', 'toolbox drawer', and 'label on a toolbox drawer' boilerplate, the claim that college courses 'use climate change as a building block', and the generic vocabulary definitions were unverified and were discarded entirely.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the boilerplate draft with source-verified content: the greenhouse-effect mechanism (shortwave in, longwave heat absorbed and re-radiated), observed changes with each source's own framing (IPCC 1.09 [0.95 to 1.20] C for 2011-2020 vs 1850-1900; NASA 1.19 C / 2.14 F above 1951-1980 in 2025 with 2024 as hottest year; Arctic sea ice about 40 percent September decline; IPCC 0.20 [0.15 to 0.25] m sea level rise 1901-2018 with rate acceleration; NOAA 8-9 inches since 1880), the IPCC's unequivocal attribution statement with calibrated likelihood terms, scenario-dependent projections (SSP1-1.9 / SSP2-4.5 / SSP5-8.5 ranges for 2081-2100 and 2100 sea level), factual impacts (hot extremes, heavy precipitation), and definitions of mitigation and adaptation with no policy advocacy.

Every quantitative claim was checked against its source text (IPCC PDFs read directly; NASA pages read live; NOAA record reused from the registry) and arithmetic was re-checked (e.g., 1.19 C x 9/5 = 2.14 F; 0.20 m = 20 cm ~ 8 inches, consistent with NOAA's 8-9 inches).
Added five source-backed practice questions with answer keys distributed across A/B/C/D (A:1, B:2, C:1, D:1).
Kept climate classification, weather, ocean circulation, and glacier mechanics out of scope per the sibling-topic map, referencing glaciers only as an observed change.
rightsIssues: All sources are authoritative primary works (IPCC reports, NASA, NOAA) used as REFERENCE_ONLY. Facts were synthesized into original prose; the only quoted passage is the short IPCC attribution sentence, attributed in text. IPCC reports are citable public summaries; NASA and NOAA content is U.S. government work. No source wording was reproduced beyond that single brief quotation and common technical terms.
